title: HIS-201 Ch. 1 — 4 Main Ideas
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 1: The First Civilizations of North America

cards.term: The characteristics of Mesoamerican civilization
cards.def: Farming surpluses let Mesoamericans build civilizations with large cities, specialized workers, social classes, monumental palaces and temples, marketplaces, schools, writing, mathematics, and accurate calendars.

cards.term: The land-bridge migration theory
cards.def: The traditional theory holds that Ice Age hunters from Asia followed megafauna across the exposed Beringia land bridge and then moved south through an ice-free corridor.

cards.term: The coastal boat migration theory
cards.def: Because glaciers may have blocked the inland route, some scholars argue that early migrants traveled in small boats down the Pacific coast.

cards.term: The multiple-migration theory
cards.def: Whole-genome evidence suggests three migrations from Siberia, with the first producing most Native Americans and later waves producing Arctic peoples and Athapaskan speakers.

cards.term: How the Paleo-Indians lived
cards.def: The Paleo-Indians lived as nomadic hunter-gatherers who followed herds of megafauna, which supplied all of their food, clothing, tools, and other material needs.

cards.term: Why the megafauna disappeared
cards.def: Post-Ice Age climate change combined with human overhunting wiped out most megafauna, forcing hunters to rely on smaller game, fishing, and gathering.

cards.term: How regional cultures arose after the Ice Age
cards.def: As receding glaciers diversified ecosystems, peoples adapted to local resources and developed distinct languages, political systems, religions, and farming and hunting patterns.

cards.term: Why agriculture was revolutionary
cards.def: Growing storable crops let people settle permanently, which allowed populations to grow, workers to specialize, social classes to form, and large cities to develop.

cards.term: How maize was developed
cards.def: Over many generations, Mesoamerican farmers repeatedly replanted the largest kernels of the wild grass teosinte until the plant became productive maize.

cards.term: The worldwide spread of American crops
cards.def: After European contact, American crops such as corn, potatoes, squash, beans, and manioc spread across Europe, Africa, and Asia and revolutionized the world's diet for better and for worse.

cards.term: How Indians used fire to reshape the environment
cards.def: Woodland Indians regularly burned underbrush, which enriched the soil, encouraged new forage, and created better conditions for the deer and other game that the Indians hunted.

cards.term: How Native Americans transformed their environments
cards.def: Native Americans reshaped their lands through vast engineering projects in central Mexico, rerouted rivers, and managed forests, disproving the romantic image of untouched nature.

cards.term: How Amazon peoples managed the rainforest
cards.def: Peoples of the Amazon encouraged the growth of trees bearing edible fruit and enriched poor soils, so much of the rainforest reflects long human management.

cards.term: How geography and climate shaped early North Americans
cards.def: Regions with abundant, reliable resources supported settled, stratified societies, while arid or harsh regions like the Great Basin and Arctic favored small, mobile bands.

cards.term: How the Pacific Northwest's abundance shaped its peoples
cards.def: Rich fisheries and forests made farming unnecessary in the Pacific Northwest, giving its peoples leisure for works of art and an elaborate social and ceremonial life.

cards.term: How the north-south axis limited the Americas
cards.def: The Americas' north-south axis created sharp climate differences that made communication and the transfer of crops and technology far harder than along Eurasia's east-west axis.

cards.term: Why maize spread slowly through North America
cards.def: Maize took thousands of years to move from Mesoamerica into the Southwest and Eastern Woodlands because each new climate required farmers to breed new varieties.

cards.term: Why the Americas lacked draft animals
cards.def: Tropical barriers kept llamas and alpacas in South America, so the civilizations of Mesoamerica had no large animals for transport, plowing, or meat.

cards.term: Why scarce domestic animals left Native Americans vulnerable to disease
cards.def: With few domesticated animals, Native Americans were never exposed to diseases that came from domesticated animals and so had little or no immunity to those diseases.

cards.term: How Eurasians gained immunity to disease
cards.def: Eurasians who survived childhood bouts of livestock-borne diseases such as smallpox and measles gained immunity, so Europeans carried diseases that their own adults resisted.

cards.term: The catastrophe after European contact
cards.def: In the decades after contact, Eurasian diseases combined with warfare, hunger, and displacement to kill Native Americans by the millions.

cards.term: The significance of the Clovis discoveries
cards.def: The Clovis and Folsom finds, confirmed by radiocarbon dating, first proved that humans lived in Ice Age America and established the first accepted chronology of American settlement.

cards.term: How the Olmec ball game resembled modern games
cards.def: Like modern sports, the Olmec ball game featured teams, a rubber ball, a marked court, spectators, and athletic stars, and the stone-ring goal recalls a basketball hoop.

cards.term: How the Olmec ball game differed from modern games
cards.def: Players struck the heavy rubber ball only with their hips, buttocks, or knees, and games carried religious meaning that could end in the sacrifice of losers.

cards.term: The myth of the Moundbuilders
cards.def: Many later white Americans wrongly credited the eastern mounds to a vanished outside race, a prejudice that denied Native peoples credit for their own monumental achievements.

cards.term: The decline and rebuilding of American societies before contact
cards.def: After many American cultures declined, the most successful new societies arose in the Caribbean and central Mexico, and both were deeply stratified.

cards.term: The most important cause of regional diversity in ancient North America
cards.def: Distinctive weather conditions, along with the Americas' immense geographic and climatic variety, were the most important cause of regional diversity among the societies of ancient North America.

cards.term: The early Americans' innovation of greatest long-term importance
cards.def: The early Americans' manipulation of certain plants into domesticated crops was their innovation of greatest long-term importance, creating farming breakthroughs that still sustain peoples around the world.

cards.term: The effect of Native American crops on Africa's population
cards.def: Native American crops such as maize and manioc may have increased Africa's population enough to offset the population losses caused by the Atlantic slave trade.

cards.term: Corn's place in American diets today
cards.def: Corn, first domesticated by Native Americans, remains the native crop most central to American diets today, feeding livestock and sweetening and thickening many processed foods.
